💡 Key Takeaways

  • Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a firm-wide technical strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Scaling Tech by Aligning Humans.

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read.

Recent findings suggest that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Scott Behrens, Principal Security Engineer at Netflix, presented how staff-plus engineers can define and align a firm-wide technical strategy. Drawing on Netflix's experience scaling internal AI agents, the talk argued that a strategy that brings people together can often scale impact further than any code an engineer could write alone.

Behrens explained that the work started when several product strategies, each with its own direction, began to share similar technical risks. Without a common technical strategy underneath them, teams were optimizing locally for different goals. His view was that technical strategy can complement product strategy without waiting for it, that lightweight strategies deliver faster than long technical documents, and that a clear north star does more steering than people expect.

Industry observers note that the talk presented a playbook organized as levels in a video game. The first step is finding the right problem. Behrens suggested looking at firm communications, incident trends, technical debt, conversations with other tech leads, and gaps between team charters, then deciding whether the problem is worth solving now, whether it is foundational or compounding, and whether one is the right person to lead it.

Industry observers note that next comes the pitch. Behrens recommended a short problem statement that explains the intent, the expected value, the problems with supporting evidence, why the work matters now, and dated next steps. He suggested leaving possible approaches open so the people who join can shape them, and testing the statement early with a few colleagues, including the likeliest dissenter.

In a recent development, the presentation then covered building a small tiger team focused on creating the strategy rather than executing it. Behrens highlighted the importance of mixing perspectives, choosing people comfortable with ambiguity, getting manager support, and agreeing on scope, timeline, and a clear stop condition from the start. He shared that his first meeting had far too many people and still missed key functions, and emphasized that the most important trait of a good team is making it safe to push back.

With a team in place, the next step is a north star, a short aspirational statement that gives direction and helps answer whether a piece of work moves the organization closer or farther from its goal. Behrens noted that writing a good north star is harder than it looks, and recommended drafting it with the team and pairing it with key outcomes that define what must be true.

In a recent development, the strategy itself, according to Behrens, is simply a set of choices. He described writing strategy bets as a choice versus another reasonable choice, naming the tradeoff explicitly, keeping each bet short, and revisiting them over time. If a bet does not feel a little uncomfortable, he said, it is probably not a real bet. Keeping only a small set of active bets helps the strategy stay focused.

It has been revealed that the talk also emphasized communication and feedback. Behrens suggested expanding support gradually from the immediate team to managers, directors, and executives, recruiting champions across the organization, and openly showing how feedback changed the strategy. Success, he said, is when you are not in the room and people can still explain the work. He also reviewed common failure modes, such as unclear problem statements, the wrong team, vague north stars, bets that are not really bets, and strategies that nobody knows exist.

The presentation concluded by encouraging engineers to keep strategy simple, communicate it widely, use a short north star to steer decisions, and adapt the playbook to their own context. As organizations launch more initiatives in parallel, especially around AI, the ability of senior engineers to align many teams around a shared technical direction may become as valuable as the systems they build.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, boodleBox notes Montana has approved it as a vendor in the state’s Master AI Products and Services procurement program.
  • The announcement is an example of a shift from individual employees experimenting with AI to institutions deciding what they can buy and how staff can use it.
  • It has been revealed that montana’s September information technology board report says its statewide AI solicitation closed with 50 vendors approved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, boodleBox notes Montana has approved it as a vendor in the state’s Master AI Products and Services procurement program. The selection gives eligible agencies, colleges and universities a route to purchase the collaborative AI workspace. It does not mean those institutions have placed orders, deployed the product or agreed to use it across the state.

The announcement is an example of a shift from individual employees experimenting with AI to institutions deciding what they can buy and how staff can use it. A department trying a chatbot may be able to start quickly. A public agency or university choosing an institutional service has more to decide: what data may enter the system, which staff can use it, what needs human review and who can see shared work.

It has been revealed that montana’s September information technology board report says its statewide AI solicitation closed with 50 vendors approved. The state estimates that buying from the resulting list can avoid roughly six months of procurement time per solicitation. That is the state’s estimate for the framework, not a measurement of savings from BoodleBox or a promise that any particular order will go through in six months less.

BoodleBox’s announcement identifies the organization as one of the approved vendors. It did not disclose a purchase value, the number of seats or a deployment schedule. Those distinctions matter because being eligible to sell gives the company access to a purchasing channel, but does not establish actual demand for its software. Montana’s procurement office describes eMACS as the state’s system for managing vendor registration, bids and contracts.

Industry observers note that boodleBox’s product documentation describes a shared workspace in which people can choose from different providers’ models or let the software select one. People can also bring several models into the same conversation. A team could, for example, ask one model to summarize a nonconfidential document and ask another to identify omissions. Those responses are starting points for human review, not independent verification of the document.

Sources indicate that coach Mode adds advice about how to frame a prompt or evaluate a response. Memory Mode can bring information from earlier chats into an answer, while a human-only messaging option lets participants discuss a problem without sending each message to a model. These controls address different needs: a training group might want suggestions to follow an answer, while a team deliberating over an internal decision may want an ordinary conversation. Default settings and sharing permissions determine whether those distinctions are easy for staff to maintain.

In a recent development, boodleBox notes its security and privacy practices distinguish between manufacturer-controlled models and those run by outside providers. In the latter case, prompts and relevant excerpts of attached material may be sent to an outside API, subject to the company’s stated data-handling rules. An institution still needs to assess what can be submitted to each model, how records are retained and whether its agreements address the kinds of information staff handle.

A practical pilot would begin with low-risk tasks and measure both usage and the quality of the result. A university might track how much time staff save drafting course materials, while an agency might count how often a model summary needs substantive correction. The vendor list makes purchasing more straightforward. Whether the software is useful and safe for a specific workflow remains a decision for the institution using it.

Industry News: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that language models can do a lot.
  • Say a customer calls your support line.
  • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they remarked (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

It has been revealed that computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

Industry observers note that it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

In a recent development, parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

In a recent development, parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

It has been revealed that downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

According to recent reports, the diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

Industry observers note that we measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

Recent findings suggest that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

Sources indicate that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's fresh is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Industry observers note that apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

It has been revealed that urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Industry observers note that emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

Recent findings suggest that the app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Industry observers note that reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

Sources indicate that you use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Recent findings suggest that raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

It has been revealed that language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

It has been revealed that each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

Sources indicate that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

In a recent development, each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

Andrew Nassar, CTO of IC Realtime – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2229 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the organization through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis.
  • Recent findings suggest that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments.
  • You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that andrew Nassar is CTO of IC Realtime, where he has helped guide the organization through shifts from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and AI-assisted video analysis. With more than 20 years in the surveillance industry, he focuses on turning advances in computer vision and edge computing into practical tools for understanding events, finding footage, and improving security operations.

Recent findings suggest that IC Realtime designs video surveillance systems and software for residential and commercial environments. Its Bunker platform adds AI analysis to compatible camera systems through a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson-powered gateway, supporting contextual alerts and natural-language video search. The platform combines local analysis with cloud-connected services for remote access and video history.

You’ve helped lead IC Realtime through the transitions from analog cameras to digital recording, remote monitoring, and now AI. What convinced you that AI could fundamentally change surveillance, and what advances have made sophisticated video analysis practical at the edge?

We have worked with machine learning and computer vision on our cameras for years. The opportunity became much more useful when the system could help someone understand an event and find the relevant footage, rather than simply produce more video to review. A homeowner wants to know what deserves attention. A business wants to find an incident without spending hours searching.

Bunker brings that approach to a dedicated NVIDIA Jetson gateway at the property. Moving core analysis closer to the cameras can reduce the dependence on sending every analytical task to the cloud and improve responsiveness. The practical advance is the combination of local computing and software that turns video into contextual alerts and searchable events.

Recent findings suggest that my standard is still proven value. The technology has to solve a real problem in the environment where the customer will use it. A good demonstration is the beginning of that process.

Using Bunker as an example, could you walk us through what happens between a camera capturing an event and a user receiving an alert? Which AI functions run locally, what still requires the cloud, and what data leaves the property?

At a high level, a compatible camera sends video to the Bunker Gateway, and core AI analysis happens on that gateway at the property. The platform links detected activity to video events and can send a contextual alert with a snapshot and a plain-language description. The user can then review the video in the app.

According to recent reports, bunker uses a hybrid architecture. Cloud connectivity supports remote access, subscription services and video history, so it would be misleading to call the platform cloud-free or to say no video leaves the property. What matters is how that data is protected when it does leave. Everything is encrypted in transit, including live video, which stays encrypted from the gateway all the way to the viewer’s screen. The infrastructure in between relays it but can’t watch it. Each gateway authenticates with its own certificate, never shared credentials, and footage stored in the cloud is encrypted.

Customers should get a clear explanation of that flow, including which features depend on the internet and what happens when the connection is down.

Security cameras operate in rain, darkness, glare, and constantly changing environments. What is the hardest real-world failure you’ve encountered, and how do you measure whether improvements reduce false alarms without increasing missed incidents?

I’ve been in this industry for more than 20 years, and camera technology has improved dramatically, especially in low light and difficult conditions. Nighttime and noisy images are now nearly as clear as daytime. Even so, rain, glare, fog and snow can still reduce an AI model’s accuracy. Better sensors don’t remove those variables.

Sources indicate that so we chose a dynamic approach that adjusts to changing environments and times of day, rather than relying on one fixed configuration. Over the past two years of development, we’ve put thousands of hours into testing in real-world installations, not just cameras on a bench, and we’ve built the system around what those deployments taught us.

Recent findings suggest that I wouldn’t judge an improvement by a lower notification count alone. The question is whether it removes irrelevant alerts while still catching the incidents that matter. Reducing noise is only valuable if the system stays useful when something important happens.

Industry observers note that detecting a person or vehicle is different from deciding that behavior is concerning. How do you define an anomaly, adapt that definition to each location, and prevent the system from treating harmless activity as a threat?

It has been revealed that A detected object does not, by itself, tell you whether there is a problem. A delivery at the front entrance and activity in a restricted area can involve the same type of object but require very different responses. The starting point should be the customer’s use case and the context of that particular property.

Recent findings suggest that I would distinguish an event worth reviewing from a conclusion that someone is a threat. The system should help a person understand what was observed and why it was surfaced, with access to the underlying footage. It should not encourage the user to treat every unfamiliar activity as evidence of wrongdoing.

According to recent reports, as these systems become more capable, the challenge is to make that context useful without overstating what the AI knows. Human judgment remains notable, particularly when an alert could lead to a consequential action.

It has been revealed that natural-language search promises to replace hours of manually reviewing footage. How does your system connect a user’s description to the right video, and how do you test for missed events, incorrect matches, or AI-generated descriptions that the footage doesn’t support?

Industry observers note that the concept is to make video searchable in the language a person would naturally use. As activity is detected, Bunker creates time-stamped descriptions associated with video events. A user’s question is used to search that indexed record and surface relevant footage. That gives the user a starting point without manually scrubbing through the entire recording.

The footage should remain the basis for checking the result. A generated description is useful for navigation, but it should not be treated as more authoritative than what the camera actually captured.

Sources indicate that for testing, I would separate three questions: Did the system miss a relevant event? Did it retrieve something that does not match the request? Did the description include something the footage does not support? Those are different failure modes. Evaluating only whether the search returns a plausible-looking answer would not be enough.

It has been revealed that what trade-offs does NVIDIA Jetson hardware impose on model size, accuracy, power consumption, and the number of camera feeds you can analyze? How do you maintain reliable performance when using older third-party cameras, reaching processing capacity, or losing internet connectivity?

The design question is how to deliver useful analysis within the resources available at the property. Model complexity, the amount of video being processed and the required response time all have to fit the gateway’s operating limits. That is why the number of supported streams alone does not tell the whole performance story.

Bunker’s launch prepares support up to 10 camera streams. Compatible ONVIF cameras let customers keep their existing hardware, but compatibility still needs to be verified for each installation. Profiles, firmware, image quality and the features being used all matter.

Recent findings suggest that we also need to be precise about resilience. Local processing and cloud-connected services are different parts of the system, and having an edge gateway doesn’t mean every feature works normally during an internet outage. Updates are part of reliability too. Every update is signed and verified on the gateway before it installs, older vulnerable versions are rejected, and a failed update rolls back automatically. A bad update shouldn’t be what takes a property’s security system offline.

It has been revealed that local inference alone doesn’t answer every privacy question. Where does Bunker store footage, search queries, and AI-generated metadata, how long are they retained, and who can access them? How do you improve your models without assuming access to customers’ private footage?

Recent findings suggest that footage and the databases behind the service are encrypted at rest. Passwords are hashed and sessions expire, so even a database breach wouldn’t give anyone working logins. The gateway itself is encrypted too, so a stolen device yields no footage and no credentials. Bunker’s launch offering included 60 days of cloud video history on Standard and 365 days on Premium, plus Video Vault for clips a customer chooses to save.

It has been revealed that we don’t use customer footage to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates of anyone the cameras capture. A customer using the product is not permission for us to reuse their private video.

According to recent reports, the controversy surrounding Flock Safety has highlighted questions about who can search surveillance data and whether access is properly revoked. Although your deployment model differs, what lessons apply to your systems, and which safeguards should be mandatory rather than optional?

The backlash against Flock isn’t really about the AI. It’s about who can get in and search the data. Much of the scrutiny came down to account security, including lawmakers asking why multi-factor authentication wasn’t mandatory. When a stolen password is enough to search a surveillance system, it doesn’t matter where the model runs.

With Bunker, the only people with access to a system’s data are the people that system’s owner has granted access. We don’t share it with third parties, we don’t use customer data to train our models, and we don’t create biometric templates.

Security has to start at the device and carry through to the account. Every Bunker gateway ships with its own cryptographic identity, so there are no default passwords to change or for an attacker to look up. Firmware is verified at every boot, updates are signed and checked before they install, and logins are protected with multi-factor authentication. Beyond that, access should be removed promptly when it’s no longer needed, and sensitive activity should leave an auditable record. Trust depends on being able to explain who did what.

According to recent reports, people captured by a camera often aren’t the people who bought it. How should AI surveillance account for the privacy of neighbors, employees, visitors, and passersby, and are there capabilities you would deliberately refuse to build?

It has been revealed that the installation needs a defined purpose, and that purpose should guide what is captured, what is analyzed and who can see the results. Wanting to secure an entrance doesn’t mean every activity on a neighboring property should become part of a searchable record.

One line we’ve drawn is identity. Bunker doesn’t create biometric templates, and it doesn’t attach an identity to anyone it detects. It describes what happened, not who someone is. That keeps the system focused on events rather than on tracking or profiling people.

More capability doesn’t automatically mean more value. If a feature creates a serious trust problem without solving a clear customer problem, that’s a reason not to build it.

Looking ahead three to five years, what meaningful capability do you expect edge AI to unlock beyond today’s detection and search—and what technical or trust problem must be solved before it deserves widespread adoption?

According to recent reports, honestly, the future of AI is uncharted right now, and it’s moving faster than anything I’ve seen in my career. We’re following those changes almost daily and looking at where they can genuinely benefit the people using our platform.

Sources indicate that the areas that matter most to us are context, understanding, and systems that keep learning and improving. The value is in helping someone understand a developing situation and decide what needs attention, instead of piecing together a string of separate notifications.

In a recent development, the technical challenge is to do that reliably in changing environments and within the limits of the local hardware. The trust challenge is to make the system’s limits and data practices easy to understand. People need to know what it observed, what it inferred and when a human needs to make the call.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore professional security cameras, recorders, and AI-powered video surveillance systems should visit IC Realtime.

Recent findings suggest that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

As a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Recent findings suggest that mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

In a recent development, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

Sources indicate that on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

In a recent development, the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Huawei Debuts OSTA Sub-Brand With AI-Centered O1 Pro Phone

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a fresh smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.
  • In a recent development, the newly introduced brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features.
  • According to recent reports, huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a newly introduced product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Huawei used its November 20, 2026 brand event to introduce OSTA (星芒), a fresh smartphone sub-brand, and launch the O1 Pro as a HarmonyOS AI phone with a starting list price of CNY 5,699.

In a recent development, the newly introduced brand’s first handset makes Huawei’s own software and assistant its defining features. The official product presentation introduces HarmonyOS 7 AI Pioneer Edition and Xiao Xingmang, an OSTA-specific interactive companion form of the Xiaoyi assistant.

According to recent reports, huawei’s Vmall listing labels the O1 Pro as a newly introduced product and lists the 12GB/256GB version at CNY 5,499, a CNY 200 discount from CNY 5,699. The range also offers 12GB/512GB, 16GB/512GB and 16GB/1TB configurations.

Huawei describes an interaction model in which the Xiaoyi AI screen is available immediately when the display is activated, using frequent usage scenarios and habits to present services proactively. Xiaoyi Space draws on likes, favorites and long-term memory, while natural-voice interaction supports continuous conversation and dialect recognition.

In a recent development, the product’s more consequential claim concerns execution. In Huawei’s coffee example, Xiaoyi uses location and preferences to recommend a drink, incorporates discounts and completes the order. Other demonstrations offer restaurant suggestions during travel, return guidance after a concert, meeting-schedule reminders and food-order pickup notifications, extending the assistant from responses into task completion and timely prompts.

It has been revealed that additional Huawei examples connect viewing records to film recommendations and post-viewing discussions, remember food preferences for personalized suggestions, and provide game information and match reminders. Together, those examples place the assistant across entertainment, dining, travel and work, with Xiao Xingmang supplying the companion interface for OSTA users.

Recent findings suggest that the official specifications list a Kirin 9030S processor and HarmonyOS 7.0, alongside a 6.39-inch OLED display with a 16:9.5 aspect ratio, 2232-by-1320 resolution and up to 120Hz refresh. The handset is 6.68mm thick and weighs about 200 grams.

The specifications also list a 7,000mAh typical-capacity battery supporting up to 66W wired and 50W wireless charging, with the chargers required for those maximum rates sold separately. The rear camera system combines a 200-megapixel optically stabilized main camera, a 50-megapixel optically stabilized periscope telephoto camera with approximately 3.7x optical zoom, and Huawei’s second-generation Hongfeng color camera.

In a recent development, for meeting capture, a four-microphone spatial array supports directional pickup. Huawei states its AI recording functions provide real-time transcription, summaries and translation, giving the phone an administrative use case beyond the consumer-oriented assistant demonstrations. The device also supports eSIM alongside two physical nano-SIM slots, although eSIM use requires carrier service.

#69499. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1312 w)

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • Industry observers note that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Industry observers note that today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

It has been revealed that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to strategy for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

In a recent development, but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

It has been revealed that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

It has been revealed that the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Sources indicate that figure 1. Latest public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

Sources indicate that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an crucial part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

In a recent development, publicly available genomic data has proved key in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support latest research that others can build upon.

Sources indicate that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Sources indicate that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an notable first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

Industry observers note that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

According to recent reports, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

According to recent reports, beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

Tech Report: Stavros Gadinis, Berkeley Law Professor and Author of Corporate Ordering – Interview Series

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law.
  • His upcoming book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled.
  • Your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stavros Gadinis is the George R. Johnson Professor of Law at UC Berkeley School of Law. His research examines corporate governance, financial regulation, and the internal systems companies use to make and monitor decisions. Before entering academia, he practiced corporate law in Europe.

His upcoming book, Corporate Ordering: How Corporations Navigate Social Conflict, published by Cambridge University Press, examines how businesses develop governance systems when public rules are unsettled. Through cases involving ridesharing, climate sustainability, and artificial intelligence, it considers how companies make rules, exercise authority, and oversee their own conduct.

Your career spans corporate legal practice in Europe and research on corporate governance and financial regulation at Berkeley Law. How did that background shape your thinking, and what inspired you to write Corporate Ordering?

I began my career practicing corporate law in Europe, and then spent many years at Berkeley studying corporate governance and financial regulation, including how rules spread across borders when no single government is in charge. We tend to think of the business world and the regulatory world as opposites, one eager for quick decisions and large profits, the other committed to bureaucratic process and the public good. Practice and research both taught me that the line is much blurrier than that.

The book grew out of conversations with general counsel and senior executives about how they handle controversial decisions, the ones where employees, customers, communities and governments all want different things. What struck me is how closely their methods resemble those of a good regulator. They gather information by reaching out to the people affected, they explain their choices publicly, and they build mechanisms to check whether those choices hold up. These are not regulatory habits or corporate habits. They are the principles of sound decisionmaking in any institution that wields power over others. Corporate Ordering is my attempt to describe that machinery, show where it works, and show where it fails.

What is “corporate ordering,” and how does it help explain the way AI companies set rules for technologies that regulation has yet to catch up with?

Industry observers note that corporate ordering is the internal governance infrastructure companies build to make contested decisions before the law tells them what to do. It has three functions, which mirror the branches of a state. Rulemaking is how a firm writes its own principles. Executive action is how it applies them to concrete decisions. Monitoring is how it checks whether it followed through, and how it finds out when it did not.

Recent findings suggest that AI companies show all three at work. The frontier labs write constitutions, model specifications and safety frameworks, which is rulemaking. They decide whether a model is ready to launch, what it will refuse and who gets access, which is executive action. And they commission red-teaming, outside evaluations and incident reporting, which is monitoring. In the book I chart these functions across the major labs. The differences are real, but so is a striking convergence, as each firm discovers why it needs every piece.

I want to be clear about one thing, because it is often misread. Corporate ordering is not an argument against regulation. It describes the material regulation will be built from. When legislators act, they borrow concepts the companies developed first. The real question is whether that first draft was written carefully enough to deserve borrowing.

Your book examines ridesharing, climate sustainability, and AI governance. Which lessons from the first two areas are most useful for AI, and where does AI present fundamentally different challenges?

Sources indicate that the lesson from ridesharing and climate is that corporations very often write the first draft of the law. Uber and Lyft developed insurance and safety reporting practices before states had rules for them, and much of corporate carbon accounting runs on the GHG Protocol, a standard business helped build. Regulators then condoned those practices, supplemented them or wrote them into law. Regulation rarely starts from a blank slate. And the more thoughtful companies are about their choices, the more they take affected parties into account, the more likely those choices are to survive into regulation.

According to recent reports, AI differs in two ways. The first is speed. Regulators are often a step behind industry, but in AI the gap is far wider. Regulators will have to look to companies to develop standards and internal processes, and concentrate their own efforts on oversight, verification and enforcement. That makes their role different, not smaller. Verification is where public power matters most, because it is where the conflict of interest with management is strongest. The second difference is reach. AI touches nearly every part of daily life, and it has become a major investment for the nation as a whole. The systemic risk implications are as hard to miss as they are to fathom.

When an AI organization selects and pays its own outside safety evaluators, what safeguards make that oversight meaningfully independent?

In a recent development, this conflict of interest is familiar from financial auditing, and corporate law already has tools to manage it. The first is who hires and fires. The relationship with the evaluator should sit with independent directors who have no other financial ties to the organization, much as the audit committee, not the CEO or CFO, oversees the external auditor. Management should not be able to dismiss a reviewer whose findings are inconvenient.

The second is access and publication. The evaluator needs to see what it asks to see, and it needs the right to publish its findings, or at least a meaningful summary, without a firm veto. Reputational risk is what gives a review its teeth. The third is common review standards, so that an evaluation means the same thing across firms and evaluators cannot compete by being lenient. The fourth is protection for whistleblowers, and even rewards when they bring actionable information, because people inside the company are often the first to know when an evaluation was steered.

It has been revealed that suppose an outside evaluator identifies a serious safety concern just before a major model launch. Who should receive that finding, and who should have the authority to delay or stop deployment?

The finding should go to the board directly, ideally to a committee of independent directors responsible for safety, and not only through the management team that is pushing for the launch. Management can and should respond, but it should not be the filter. The authority to delay or stop deployment should rest with the board, because this is exactly the kind of decision boards exist to make, one with large stakes, conflicting interests and no obvious right answer.

Sources indicate that but the more key point is that the decision must be explicit and documented, and traceable to the people who made it. If the board goes ahead despite the concern, the record should show what it knew, what it weighed and why it judged the risk acceptable. That paper trail creates the conditions for liability, or at least reputational damage, and it makes people think twice. Courts are increasingly willing to recognize that design choices in software have consequences for owners, and a company that can show a serious, documented effort stands in a very different position from one that cannot.

When safety concerns conflict with revenue targets or competitive pressure, what should a credible board decision-making process look like?

A credible process is an informed one, and it leaves a record. The board should see concrete information about the costs of delay, the nature and likelihood of the safety concern, and the options for mitigating it. It should ask whether the testing was adequate and, where it was not, commission more or invite outside review. Where real uncertainty remains, there are options between launching and shelving, such as a limited release, a staged rollout or a sandbox, that let the tech giant learn more before it commits. And whatever the board decides, what the company then says publicly about the model’s safety must be accurate, which is where much of the current litigation risk lies.

Then the board should write down what it decided and why. Over time those records become a body of precedent, so the next hard call is measured against the last one, and anyone reviewing the manufacturer can see whether its stated principles actually bind. Microsoft has started to build this kind of decision record, and I think it is one of the most underrated tools in AI governance. Competitive pressure is real, and a board may reasonably decide to move ahead. What it cannot do is decide by default.

Your work proposes a “social business judgment” standard for evaluating board decisions. How would that apply to an AI manufacturer that postpones a profitable product launch because of potential public harm?

Under existing corporate law, a board that postpones a profitable launch is already well protected. Courts defer to directors’ business judgment, and accepting lower profits today to avoid harm tomorrow fits comfortably within it. The harder question runs the other way, whether the board took public harm seriously at all.

In a recent development, social business judgment asks the board to evaluate potential public harm the way it evaluates any other business risk, through tangible, measurable and specific metrics wherever possible. The emphasis is on process and due diligence, not on the outcome. A board that sources the right information, hears from those affected and records its reasoning has earned deference, whether it postpones the launch or proceeds with it. A board that does none of this has not. So in the case you describe, the postponement itself is not the issue. The issue is whether the board can show how it reached that decision, and whether it would reach the same one again on the same facts.

Recent findings suggest that AI companies publish safety frameworks and voluntary commitments, but readers rarely see how those policies affect individual decisions. What evidence would distinguish effective governance from a public relations exercise?

Industry observers note that very often, when companies publish frameworks, the public is left wondering whether the framework ever applies to specific decisions or remains rhetoric the company never follows through on. The answer is disclosure of a particular kind. Rather than more statements of principle, companies should report the specific choices they made and how the framework shaped them, which launches were delayed, which capabilities were held back, which risk thresholds were triggered and what followed.

It has been revealed that the most telling evidence is a decision that cost the tech giant something. A framework that has never changed an outcome, never delayed a launch and never been invoked against revenue is hard to distinguish from public relations. These disclosures also need to be specific enough to verify, and for the most consequential questions they should be verified by a third party with the standing to say so publicly.

It has been revealed that where does corporate self-governance reach its limits? Which decisions about acceptable AI risk require public rules or democratic oversight?

According to recent reports, the most key limit has to do with failures to monitor. Even a well-intentioned, responsible organization can face a major crisis, and at that moment conflicts of interest multiply. Employees may withhold information that would hurt their jobs or their bonuses. Executives may suppress bad news to avoid public criticism. Fear of lawsuits may keep the company from being open. In past corporate crises, the crucial information usually came from people leadership could not control, external auditors and reviewers, affected parties, or internal whistleblowers using independent reporting channels.

Sources indicate that this is where public rules matter most. The law can add relatively little at the rulemaking stage, because statutes tend to borrow their key concepts from the companies. It can add more on disclosure, by reaching firms that will not disclose voluntarily. And it adds the most on verification, by requiring independent review, protecting whistleblowers and giving outside checks real authority.

The other limit is collective. The most a single organization can do is stop itself. It cannot stop its competitors. Decisions about catastrophic risk, including whether to slow the frontier, require coordination across firms and governments, at home and internationally. One model I find promising is an international standard-setter along the lines of the ISSB in sustainability reporting, independent of governments but overseen by trustees that include them. Corporate ordering is necessary for this work, because the taming of these models happens inside the companies that build them, but it cannot carry the work alone.

If you were advising the board of a fast-growing AI manufacturer today, what three governance changes would you prioritize, and what evidence would you look for a year later to determine whether they worked?

First, outreach in rulemaking. Before adopting or revising its safety framework or usage policies, the organization should consult the people affected (users, civil society, domain experts) and publish what it heard and how it responded. Second, regular responsibility reporting, an annual account of the hard decisions the board and management made under the framework, with enough detail to be checked. Third, an external monitor, hired by and reporting to independent directors, with full access and the right to publish.

In a recent development, A year later I would look for evidence that each one actually bit. For outreach, at least one rule that changed because of what the company heard. For reporting, disclosed decisions the company would rather not have discussed, including ones that cost it revenue or time. For the monitor, findings the company did not want, and a record of what the board did about them. If after a year everything reported is good news, the changes have not worked.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore the book and purchase options should visit the official website for Corporate Ordering.

It has been revealed that antoine is a visionary leader and founding partner of Unite.AI, driven by an unwavering passion for shaping and promoting the future of AI and robotics. A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Sources indicate that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks.

Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.

Grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

In a recent development, the release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana indicates managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

Recent findings suggest that cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

According to recent reports, variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

It has been revealed that teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where customers add the shared controls.

Notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

Users can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

Grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

The release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard plans let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The plan covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

In a recent development, grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs notes the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the newly introduced appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed users can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

Tech Report: OpenAI Introduces MedChemBench for Medicinal-Chemistry Reasoning

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (991 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite
